From Latin cyta, from Ancient Greek κύτος (kútos, “vessel”).

From Latin -phagia, from Ancient Greek -φαγία (-phagía), from Ancient Greek φαγεῖν (phageîn, “to eat”).
From Latin -phila, from Ancient Greek φίλος (phílos, “dear, beloved”).

parole.significato: -eum (Noun-forming suffix found in words of Greek origin meaning “place or building associated with a specific purpose…
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle French -ee m, from Latin -ēum n, from Ancient Greek -εῖον n (-eîon), originating in the substantivized neuter of -εῖος (-eîos, adjective suffix).

parole.significato: ending found in male names from Greek
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle French -ee m.
From Latin abacus.

parole.significato: an abbot, the head of an abbey
parole.testo: Inherited from Old French abé, borrowed from Latin abbātem, from Ancient Greek ἀββᾶ (abbâ), from Aramaic אבא (’abbā, “father”). Compare English abbot.
Borrowed from Latin absinthium.
Borrowed from Latin acadēmicus, from Ancient Greek ἀκαδημικός (akadēmikós).
Calqued or borrowed from Latin accentus acūtus (“sharp accent”), itself a calque of Ancient Greek προσῳδία ὀξύς (prosōidía oxús, “sharp accent”).
Coined by physicist Joseph Sauveur, from Latin acousticus, from Ancient Greek ἀκουστικός (akoustikós), from ἀκούω (akoúō, “hear”).

parole.significato: acrostic (text in which certain letters spell out a name or message)
parole.testo: From Latin acrostichis, from Ancient Greek ἀκροστιχίς (akrostikhís).
From Latin adytum, from Ancient Greek ἄδυτον (áduton).
From Middle French agathe, from Latin achatēs, from Ancient Greek ἀχάτης (akhátēs, “agate”).
From Latin Agathyrsi, from Ancient Greek Ἀγάθυρσοι (Agáthursoi).
Borrowed from Latin agōnia, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ἀγωνία (agōnía).
Borrowed, through Latin agoranomus, from Ancient Greek ἀγορανόμος (agoranómos, “clerk of the market”).
From Latin agoraphobia, from Ancient Greek ἀγορά (agorá, “gathering of people or place of gathering”) + φόβος (phóbos, “fear”).
Inherited from Old French air, aire, from Latin āēr.
Inherited from Middle French albastre, from Old French alabastre, aubastre, from Latin alabaster, alabastrum, from Ancient Greek ἀλάβαστρος (alábastros).
From Latin Alcaicus, from Ancient Greek Ἀλκαϊκός (Alkaïkós), from Ἀλκαῖος (Alkaîos, “Alcaeus”) + -ικός (-ikós, “-ic”). By surface analysis, Alcée + -ique.

parole.significato: capable of counteracting a poison; antidotal, alexipharmic
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin alexipharmacon (“antidote for a poison”), itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀλεξιφάρμακος (alexiphármakos, “antidote”).
Inherited from Old French allegorie, from Latin allegoria, from Ancient Greek ἀλληγορία (allēgoría).
Learned borrowing from Latin allēgoricus.
Borrowed from Latin aloe, Ancient Greek ἀλόη (alóē).
From alpha + privatif, from Latin alpha prīvātīvum, from Ancient Greek ἄλφα στερητικόν (álpha sterētikón).
Learned borrowing from Latin althaea, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀλθαία (althaía).
Borrowed from Latin ambrosia (“food of the gods”), from Ancient Greek ἀμβροσία (ambrosía, “of the gods”).
Borrowed from Latin amiantus, from Ancient Greek ἀμίαντος (amíantos).
Learned borrowing from Latin amphibologia, from Ancient Greek ἀμφιβολία (amphibolía, “ambiguity”).
Borrowed from Latin Amphictyones, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek Ἀμφικτύονες (Amphiktúones), both of which are only attested in the plural.
Learned borrowing from Latin amphitheātrum, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀμφιθέᾱτρον (amphithéātron).
From Latin anabaptismus, from Ancient Greek ἀνα (ana) "thorough" + Ancient Greek βάπτισμα (báptisma) "baptism".
Learned borrowing from Latin anadiplosis, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ἀναδίπλωσις (anadíplōsis).
From Middle French analogie, from Latin analogia, from Ancient Greek ἀναλογία (analogía), from ἀνα- (ana-) + λόγος (lógos, “speech, reckoning”).
Learned borrowing from Latin analyticus, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀναλυτικός (analutikós).
Borrowed from Latin anapaestus, from Ancient Greek ἀνάπαιστος (anápaistos, “reversed; anapest”).
From Latin anastasis.
Borrowed from Latin anathema, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ἀνάθεμα (anáthema).

parole.significato: Androphagi (an ancient nation of anthropophagi (cannibals) north of Scythia, recorded by Herodotus)
parole.testo: From Latin Androphagi, from Ancient Greek Ἀνδροφάγοι (Androphágoi).
From Old French anet (ca. 1300), a borrowing from Latin anēthum, from Ancient Greek ἄνηθον (ánēthon).
Unadapted borrowing from Latin angelus. Doublet of ange.
Inherited from Old French anis, from Latin anīsum, from Ancient Greek ἄνισον (ánison).
From Latin anōmalos, from Ancient Greek ἀνώμαλος (anṓmalos, “uneven, irregular, anomalous”).
Inherited from Old French antartique, from Latin antarcticus, from Ancient Greek ἀνταρκτικός (antarktikós).
Learned borrowing from Latin anthrōpophagus (“cannibal, man-eater”), itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀνθρωποφάγος (anthrōpophágos). By surface analysis, anthropo- + -phage.
Borrowed from Latin antidotum.
From Latin antinomia, from Ancient Greek ἀντινομία (antinomía).
From Latin antipathia, from Ancient Greek ἀντιπάθεια (antipátheia).
Borrowed from Latin antrum, from Ancient Greek ἄντρον (ántron).
From Latin apathīa, from Ancient Greek ἀπάθεια (apátheia).
Borrowed from Latin aphorismus, from Ancient Greek ἀφορισμός (aphorismós, “pithy phrase containing a general truth”).
Borrowed from Latin apnoea, from Ancient Greek ἄπνοια (ápnoia).
From Latin apocalypsis, from Ancient Greek ἀποκάλυψις (apokálupsis).
Borrowed from Latin apodicticus, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ἀποδεικτικός (apodeiktikós).

parole.significato: apogee (a point in an orbit around the Earth)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin apogaeum, from Ancient Greek ἀπόγειον (apógeion, “away from Earth”), from ἀπό (apó, “away”) + γῆ (gê, “Earth”).
From Latin apologus, from Ancient Greek ἀπόλογος (apólogos).
From Latin apoplēcticus, from Ancient Greek ἀποπληκτικός (apoplēktikós).
Borrowed from Latin aposiopesis, from Ancient Greek ἀποσιώπησις (aposiṓpēsis), from ἀποσιωπάω (aposiōpáō, “to be silent”).
Learned borrowing from Latin apostasia, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀποστασία (apostasía, “withdrawl, defection”).

From Latin apostrophus, from Ancient Greek ἀπόστροφος (apóstrophos, “accent of elision”), a noun use of an adjective from ἀποστρέφω (apostréphō, “to turn away”), from ἀπό (apó, “away from”) + στρέφω (stréphō, “to turn”).
Borrowed from Latin apostropha, apostrophe, from Ancient Greek ἀποστροφή (apostrophḗ), from ἀποστρέφω (apostréphō, “to turn away”), from ἀπό (apó) + στρέφω (stréphō, “to turn”).
Learned borrowing from Latin apotheōsis, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ἀποθέωσις (apothéōsis).
Learned borrowing from Latin Arabs.
Inherited from Old French orchal, from Latin aurīchalcum, modified based on aurum (“gold”) from orīchalcum (“yellow copper ore”), borrowed from Ancient Greek ὀρείχαλκος (oreíkhalkos).
Inherited from Old French archangle, borrowed from Latin archangelus, from Ancient Greek ἀρχάγγελος (arkhángelos) from ἀρχ- (arkh-) + ἄγγελος (ángelos, “messenger”).
Borrowed from Latin archīāter, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ἀρχιατρός (arkhiatrós).
Inherited from Middle French architecte, from Latin architectus, from Ancient Greek ἀρχιτέκτων (arkhitéktōn, “master builder”), from ἀρχι- (arkhi-, “chief”) + τέκτων (téktōn, “builder”).
Borrowed from Latin archontem, accusative of archōn, from Ancient Greek ἄρχων (árkhōn).
Borrowed from Latin archetypum, from archetypus, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ἀρχέτυπος (arkhétupos).
From Latin Argonauta from Ancient Greek Ἀργοναύτης (Argonaútēs) from Ἀργώ (Argṓ, “the ship Argo”) + ναύτης (naútēs, “sailor”).
Inherited from Middle French aristocratie, borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀριστοκρατίᾱ (aristokratíā, “the rule of the best”).
Learned borrowing from Latin arithmeticus (“arithmetical”), itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀριθμητικός (arithmētikós, “arithmetical”). Attested circa 1370.
Inherited from Old French ermoize, from Latin artemisia, from Ancient Greek ἀρτεμισία (artemisía), from Ἄρτεμις (Ártemis, “Artemis, the goddess”).

parole.significato: seasoning, herb, spice, especially one with a strong, pleasant odour
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin arōmatem (“spice, herb”), from Ancient Greek ἄρωμα (árōma).
From Latin arrha (“wages”), truncation of arrhabō (“down payment”), from Ancient Greek ἀρραβών (arrhabṓn, “down payment, guarantee”), from Hebrew ערבון (erabon, “guarantee”).
Inherited from Old French artere, artaire, borrowed from Latin artēria, from Ancient Greek ἀρτηρία (artēría).

parole.significato: Any one of the Artemides (the seven daughters of the Semitic goddess Astarte as mentioned by Eusebius (quoting Philo of…
parole.testo: From Latin Artemidem, accusative of Artemis, from Ancient Greek Ἄρτεμις (Ártemis). Compare Italian Artemide.

parole.significato: Areopagus (supreme judicial and legislative council of Athens)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Areopagus, from Ancient Greek Ἄρειος Πάγος (Áreios Págos, literally “Rock of Ares”).
Borrowed from Latin arōma, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ἄρωμα (árōma).
Borrowed from Latin asbestos.
From Latin Asclēpiadēus (“of or relating to Asclepiades of Samos; Asclepiadean”), from Ancient Greek Ἀσκληπιάδειος (Asklēpiádeios), from Ἀσκληπιάδης (Asklēpiádēs, “Asclepiades”) + -ειος (-eios).
Borrowed from Latin Āsiarcha, from Ancient Greek Ἀσιάρχης (Asiárkhēs).
Borrowed from Latin āsiāticus, from Ancient Greek Ἀσιατικός (Asiatikós).

From Latin asylum, from Ancient Greek ἄσυλον (ásulon, “sanctuary”) + Latin polīticus (“of or relating to civil policy”), from Ancient Greek πολῑτῐκός (polītĭkós, “civic, constitutional, public”). Equivalent to asile (“asylum”) + politique (“political”). Compare English political asylum, German polit

parole.significato: asparagus (any of various perennial plants of the genus Asparagus having leaflike stems, scalelike leaves, and small fl…
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin asparagus, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀσπάραγος (aspáragos).
From Middle French aster, from Latin astēr, from Ancient Greek ᾰ̓στήρ (ăstḗr). Doublet of star.
From Latin āsthma, from Ancient Greek ἆσθμα (âsthma).
Borrowed from Latin astrum, from Ancient Greek ἄστρον (ástron).

Borrowed from Latin astrologia (“astronomy”) (equivalent to astro- + -logie), from Ancient Greek ἀστρολογία (astrología, “telling of the stars”), from ἄστρον (ástron, “star”) + -λογία (-logía, “treating of”), combination form of -λόγος (-lógos, “one who speaks (in a certain manner)”).
Inherited from Middle French astronomie, from Old French astronomie, borrowed from Latin astronomia (“astronomy”), from Ancient Greek ἀστρονομία (astronomía). By surface analysis, astro- + -nomie.

parole.significato: Astypalaia (an island of the Dodecanese, Greece)
parole.testo: From Latin Astypalaea, from Ancient Greek Ἀστυπάλαια (Astupálaia).
From Latin asteria, from Ancient Greek ἀστήρ (astḗr), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂stḗr.
Borrowed from Latin asyndeton, from Ancient Greek ἀσύνδετον (asúndeton).
Learned borrowing from Latin āthlēta, borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀθλητής (athlētḗs), from ᾱ̓θλέω (āthléō, “to contend”) + -τής (-tḗs, masculine agentive suffix).

parole.significato: athletic (having a muscular, well developed body, being in shape)
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle French athletique, a learned borrowing from Latin āthlēticus, borrowed from Ancient Greek ᾱ̓θλητῐκός (āthlētĭkós), from ἀθλητής (athlētḗs, “athlete”) + -ικός (-ikós, adjective suffix). By surface analysis, athlète + -ique.
From Latin atheos, from Ancient Greek ἄθεος (átheos).

parole.significato: a type of high school; atheneum
parole.testo: From Latin Athenaeum, from Ancient Greek Ἀθηναῖον (Athēnaîon), from Ἀθήνη (Athḗnē, “Athena”).
Inherited from Middle French athome, borrowed from Latin atomus, from Ancient Greek ἄτομος (átomos).
Learned borrowing from Latin ātra bīlis, itself a calque of Ancient Greek μελαγχολία (melankholía).
From Latin Atropatēnus, from Ancient Greek Ἀτροπατηνός (Atropatēnós). By surface analysis, Atropatès + -ène.

parole.significato: of or relating to Atropates; only used in Médie atropatène
parole.testo: From Latin Atropatēnus, from Ancient Greek Ἀτροπατηνός (Atropatēnós), from Ἀτροπάτης (Atropátēs, “Atropates”) + -ηνός (-ēnós). By surface analysis, Atropatès + -ène.
Learned borrowing from Latin ātrophīa, from Ancient Greek ἀτροφία (atrophía, “a wasting away”).
Learned borrowing from Latin atticismos, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ᾰ̓ττῐκῐσμός (ăttĭkĭsmós).
From Latin atticus, from Ancient Greek Ἀττικός (Attikós).

From Latin austērus (“dry, harsh, sour, tart”), from Ancient Greek αὐστηρός (austērós, “bitter, harsh”), having the specific meaning "making the tongue dry" (originally used of fruits, wines), related to αὔω (aúō, “to singe”), αὖος (aûos, “dry”).
From Latin authenticus, from Ancient Greek αὐθεντικός (authentikós).
Borrowed from Latin autographum, in turn from Ancient Greek αὐτόγραφον (autógraphon, “a writing in one’s own hand”). By surface analysis, auto- + -graphe.
Borrowed from Latin azymus, from Ancient Greek ἄζυμος (ázumos).
Borrowed from Latin balanus, from Ancient Greek βάλανος (bálanos, “acorn”). Cognate with Catalan bàlan, Italian balano, Portuguese bálano, Spanish bálano.
Inherited from Old French baleine, borrowed from Latin bālaena, from Ancient Greek φάλαινα (phálaina).
From Latin ballista, from Ancient Greek βαλλίστρα (ballístra), from βάλλω (bállō, “to throw”).

Inherited from Old French base, from Latin basis, from Ancient Greek βάσις (básis).

parole.significato: the guild of legal clerks of the Paris court system under the pre-revolutionary French monarchy, from among whom legal…
parole.testo: Inherited from Old French basoche, besoiche, from Latin basilica, from Ancient Greek βασιλική (basilikḗ). The phonetic evolution was special in this case, as the expected result would be *baseuche (cf. the place name La Bazeuge). Doublet of the borrowing basilique.
Inherited from Old French basme, from Latin balsamum, a borrowing from Ancient Greek βάλσαμον (bálsamon).

Inherited from Middle French beurre (16th c.), from a regional (eastern or western) variant of burre, from Old French burre, bure, from Latin būtȳrum, from Ancient Greek βούτῡρον (boútūron, “butter”, literally “cow-cheese”).
Inherited from Middle French bibliotheque, borrowed from Latin bibliothēca (“library”), originally from Ancient Greek βιβλιοθήκη (bibliothḗkē, “book-room”). Morphologically biblio- + -thèque.
From bio- + -graphie, from Latin biographia, from Ancient Greek βιογραφία (biographía), composed by βίος (bíos, “life”) + γράφω (gráphō, “write”).
Learned borrowing from Latin bolis, from Ancient Greek βολίς (bolís).
From Middle French bombarde (“a bombard, mortar, catapult"; also "a bassoon-like musical instrument”), from Latin bombus (“buzzing; booming”).
From bombyx + -ique. Ultimately from Latin bombyx, from Ancient Greek βόμβυξ (bómbux).
From Latin bombyx, from Ancient Greek βόμβυξ (bómbux).
Borrowed from Latin boreālis (“northern”), from Boreās, from Ancient Greek Βορέᾱς (Boréās, “personification of the north wind”).
Borrowed from Latin branchia, from Ancient Greek βράγχια (bránkhia, “gills”).

Inherited from Middle French bras, from Old French bras, from Latin brachium, bracchium, from Ancient Greek βραχίων (brakhíōn). Displaced Old French feminine noun brace, ultimately from the same Latin and Ancient Greek roots.
From Middle French brione, from Latin bryōnia (“bryony”), from Ancient Greek βρυωνία (bruōnía, “bryony”).
Borrowed from Latin bulbus, from Ancient Greek βολβός (bolbós, “plant with round swelling on underground stem”).
From Latin Bebrycem, accusative of Bebryx, from Ancient Greek Βέβρυξ (Bébrux). Cognate with Italian Bebrice, bebrice.
Learned borrowing from Latin cachecticus, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek καχεκτικός (kakhektikós).
Learned borrowing of Latin cadmīa, from Ancient Greek καδμεία (kadmeía). Compare calamine.
Borrowed from Latin calamus, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek κάλαμος (kálamos). Doublet of the inherited chaume.
From Latin chalcēdōnius, from Ancient Greek χαλχηδόνιος (khalkhēdónios), cognate to Arabic كَرْكَنْد (karkand)
Borrowed from Latin calix, calicem, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek κύλιξ (kúlix). Compare also the inherited Old French chalice.

parole.testo: Unknown origin, however, most likely early 19th century. Learned borrowing from Latin chamaeleōn, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek χᾰμαιλέων (khămailéōn).
Borrowed from Latin cannabis, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek κάνναβις (kánnabis). Doublet of chanvre.
Borrowed from Latin canna (“reed”), from Ancient Greek κάννα (kánna, “reed”), from Akkadian 𒄀 (/⁠qanû⁠/, “reed”), from Sumerian 𒄀𒈾 (gi.na).
Inherited from Old French canon, borrowed from Latin canōn, from Ancient Greek κανών (kanṓn, “measuring rod, standard”). The 'attractive person' sense comes from an ellipsis of canon de beauté.
Learned borrowing from Latin character, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek χαρακτήρ (kharaktḗr, “type, nature, character”).
Inherited from Old French cardamome, from Latin cardamomum, from Ancient Greek καρδάμωμον (kardámōmon).
Borrowed from Latin carōta, from Ancient Greek κᾰρωτόν (kărōtón).
Learned borrowing from Latin charta, from Ancient Greek χάρτης (khártēs). Cognate with French charte.

Inherited from Middle French castor, from Old French castor, borrowed from Latin castor, itself from Ancient Greek κάστωρ (kástōr). Though borrowed into French early on, the word remained a more learned term at first, while bièvre was the popular synonym.
From Latin catachrēsis, from Ancient Greek κατάχρησις (katákhrēsis).
Learned borrowing from Latin cataclysmus, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek κατακλυσμός (kataklusmós).
Borrowed from Latin catastropha, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek καταστροφή (katastrophḗ).
From Latin catholicus, from Ancient Greek καθολικός (katholikós).
Borrowed from Latin cathedra, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek καθέδρα (kathédra). Doublet of chaire and chaise.

From Latin catēchīzāre (“to instruct in religion; to catechize”), from Ancient Greek κατηχίζω (katēkhízō, “to instruct orally”), from κατηχέω (katēkhéō, “to resound, instruct orally”), from κατά (katá, “down”) + ἠχή (ēkhḗ, “sound, noise”).
Learned borrowing from Latin catēchēsis, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek κατήχησις (katḗkhēsis).
Learned borrowing from Latin catēchēticus, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek κατηχητικός (katēkhētikós).

parole.significato: caustic (capable of burning, corroding or destroying organic tissue)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin causticus (“burning”), from the Ancient Greek καυστικός (kaustikós, “burning”).
Learned borrowing from Latin cautērium, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek καυτήριον (kautḗrion).

parole.significato: Celtic (of the Celts; of the style of the Celts)
parole.testo: From Latin Celticus, from Ancient Greek Κελτικός (Keltikós). By surface analysis, Celte (“Celt”) + -ique.
From Old French centre (13th c.), a borrowing from Latin centrum, from Ancient Greek κέντρον (kéntron, “sharp point”).
Borrowed from Latin cestus.
Inherited from Middle French chaire, from Old French chaiere, chaere, inherited from Latin cathedra (“seat”), from Ancient Greek καθέδρα (kathédra). Doublet of cathèdre and chaise.

Originally, simply a variant of chaire. From Middle French chaire, inherited from Latin cathedra (“seat”), a borrowing from Ancient Greek καθέδρα (kathédra). The change -r- > -s-, while being common in the past, has been only preserved on this word and besicles. Doublet of chaire and cathèdre.
From Latin Chalcidicus, from Ancient Greek Χαλκιδικός (Khalkidikós). By surface analysis, Chalcide + -ique.
From Middle French Chaldee, from Latin chaldaeus, from Ancient Greek Χαλδαῖος (Khaldaîos).

parole.significato: a chamber in its various senses, including:
parole.testo: Inherited from Old French chambre, cambre, from Latin cambra, Medieval spelling of Latin camera (“room”), from Ancient Greek καμάρα (kamára, “something with an arched cover: a covered wagon, a covered boat, a vaulted chamber”). Doublet of caméra, a borrowing.
Borrowed from Latin chaos, from Ancient Greek χάος (kháos).
Inherited from Old French chaume, from Latin calamus, from Ancient Greek κάλαμος (kálamos). Doublet of the borrowed calame.
Borrowed from Latin chiasmus, from Ancient Greek χιασμός (khiasmós).

Inherited from Latin chilias (“the number 1000, a group of 1000 things”), from Ancient Greek χιλιάς (khiliás, “the number 1000, any large amount, a millennium”), from χῑ́λιοι (khī́lioi, “1000”) + -ᾰ́ς (-ắs, “-ad: forming collective nouns”). Equivalent to chilia- + -ade.
Learned borrowing from Latin chiliarchia, from Ancient Greek χιλιαρχία (khiliarkhía).
Borrowed from Latin chirurgia, from chirurgus, from Ancient Greek χειρουργός (kheirourgós).

Inherited from Middle French chirurgien, from Old French cirurgiien (see also Old French surgien, inherited through Vulgar Latin), or simply formed from the root of chirurgie, borrowed from Latin chīrūrgia, from chīrūrgus, from Ancient Greek χειρουργός (kheirourgós).
From Latin chōrographus, from Ancient Greek χωρογράφος (khōrográphos). By surface analysis, choro- + -graphe.
Borrowed from Latin chorus, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek χορός (khorós). Doublet of chœur.
From Latin chōrepiscopus, from Ancient Greek χωρεπίσκοπος (khōrepískopos).
Borrowed from Latin chrōmaticus, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek χρωματικός (khrōmatikós).

parole.significato: chronic (that which continues over an extended period of time)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin chronicus, from Ancient Greek χρονικός (khronikós, “of time”), from χρόνος (khrónos, “time”).

Inherited from Middle French huyle, from Old French oile, from Latin oleum, from olea (“olive”), from Ancient Greek ἐλαία (elaía, “olive”). The h was added in Middle French to indicate that the u was a vowel, as in typography u and v were used interchangeably at the time. Compare huit (“eight”).

From Old French uistre, oistre, from Latin ostrea, from Ancient Greek ὄστρεον (óstreon). The h is unetymological (no h in the Latin ostrea), but it used to disambiguate the pronunciation in the times when u and v were variants of the same letter, cf. huit, huile.
Learned borrowing from Latin hyraulicus, from Ancient Greek ὑδραυλικός (hudraulikós).
Borrowed from Latin hydra, from Ancient Greek ὕδρα (húdra).
Borrowed from Latin hydromel, hydromeli, from hydro- (from Ancient Greek ὕδωρ (húdōr, “water”)) + mel (“honey”).
From Latin Hygīa, from Ancient Greek Ὑγιεία (Hugieía).
From Middle French hymen, from Latin hymēn (“hymen”), from Ancient Greek ὑμήν (humḗn, “skin; membrane”).

Inherited from Middle French hymne, hynne, from Old French ymne m or f, from Latin hymnus m, from Ancient Greek ὕμνος m (húmnos). Formerly pronounced /in/ (as still in automne, damner); the modern pronunciation under influence of the spelling.
Borrowed from Latin hymenaeus, from Ancient Greek ὑμέναιος (huménaios).
From modern Latin hyoides, from Ancient Greek ὑοειδής (huoeidḗs, “shaped like the letter υ (u)”).
Borrowed from Latin hypallage, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ὑπαλλαγή (hupallagḗ).
From Middle French hyperbole, yperbole, a learned borrowing from Latin hyperbolē, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ὑπερβολή (huperbolḗ, “excess, exaggeration”).
Learned borrowing from Latin hyperbolicus, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ὑπερβολικός (huperbolikós). By surface analysis, hyperbole + -ique.
Borrowed from Latin hypocaustum, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ὑπόκαυστον (hupókauston).
Borrowed from Latin hypothēca (“pledge given as surety for a loan”), from Ancient Greek ὑποθήκη (hupothḗkē).

parole.significato: hypotenuse (the side of a right triangle opposite the right angle)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin hypotēnūsa, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ὑποτείνουσα (hupoteínousa).

parole.significato: Hyrcan, Hyrcanian (native or inhabitant of Hyrcania)
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle French Hyrcan, from Latin Hyrcānus, from Ancient Greek Ὑρκανός (Hurkanós).
From Latin hyaena, from Ancient Greek ὕαινα (húaina).
From Latin Heauton Timorumenos, name of a play by Terence, from Ancient Greek ἑαυτόν (heautón) + τιμωρούμενος (timōroúmenos). Popularized in a poem of the same name by Charles Baudelaire.
Learned borrowing from Latin helix, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ἕλιξ (hélix).
Learned borrowing from Latin hēmicyclium, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ἡμικύκλιον (hēmikúklion).
From Latin haemorrhagia, from Ancient Greek αἱμορραγία (haimorrhagía, “a violent bleeding”).

14th century, borrowed from Latin hērōs, from Ancient Greek ἥρως (hḗrōs). The aspiration is secondary and originated in the desire to avoid les héros sounding like les zéros. The related words remain unaspirated. Displaced Middle French heroe, borrowed from the Latin accusative hērōem.
From Latin hērōina, from late (2nd century) Ancient Greek ἡρωΐνη (hērōḯnē), feminine to ἥρως (hḗrōs, “hero”) "hero, demigod". By surface analysis, héros + -ine.

parole.significato: heresy (doctrine held by a member of a religion at variance or conflict with established religious beliefs)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old French heresie, borrowed from Latin haeresis, from Ancient Greek αἵρεσις (haíresis, “choice, system of principles”).
Borrowed from Latin iconicus, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek εἰκονικός (eikonikós). Morphologically, from icône + -ique.
Borrowed from Latin icterus, from Ancient Greek ἴκτερος (íkteros).
From Old French idiot (cf. also the older form idiote), borrowed from Latin idiōta, from Ancient Greek ἰδιώτης (idiṓtēs, “layman”) from ἴδιος (ídios, “private”).

parole.significato: idol (graven image or representation of anything that is revered, or believed to convey spiritual power)
parole.testo: From Latin īdōlum.
Learned borrowing from Latin īdōlolatrēs (with haplology), itself borrowed from Ancient Greek εἰδωλολάτρης (eidōlolátrēs).
Borrowed from Latin idea (“a (Platonic) idea; archetype”), from Ancient Greek ἰδέα (idéa, “notion, pattern”).
From Latin Idaeus (from Ancient Greek Ἰδαῖος (Idaîos)) + -en.
From Latin Helotes, from Ancient Greek Εἵλωτες (Heílōtes).
Borrowed from Latin iris, Ancient Greek ἶρις (îris).
Borrowed from Latin īrōnīa, from Ancient Greek εἰρωνεία (eirōneía).
Borrowed from Latin ithyphallus, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ἰθύφαλλος (ithúphallos).
From Latin gagātem (“jet”), from Ancient Greek Γαγάτης (Gagátēs, “lignite, jet”, literally “stone of Gagas”).
Learned borrowing from Latin iūdaismus, from Ancient Greek Ἰουδαϊσμός (Ioudaïsmós). By surface analysis, Juda + -ïsme.
Inherited from Middle French juif, backformation from Old French juive, juiue, feminine of juiu, from Latin iūdaeus, from Ancient Greek Ἰουδαῖος (Ioudaîos), from Hebrew יְהוּדִי (y'hudí).
From Latin lamia, from Ancient Greek Λάμια (Lámia).
Inherited from Middle French lampe, from Old French lampe, from Latin lampas, from Ancient Greek λαμπάς (lampás, “lamp, flambeau”).
From Latin Laodicēnus, from Ancient Greek Λαοδικηνός (Laodikēnós). By surface analysis, Laodicée + -ène.
Unadapted borrowing from Latin larynx, from Ancient Greek λάρυγξ (lárunx).
From Latin lāicus (“lay, layman, laic, laical”), from Ancient Greek λαϊκός (laïkós, “of the people”), from λαός (laós, “the people”). Doublet of lai (“lay, not belonging to the clergy”).
Borrowed from the Latin lemma, itself a borrowing from the Ancient Greek λῆμμᾰ (lêmmă).
From Latin Laestrȳgōn, from Ancient Greek Λαιστρῡ́γων (Laistrū́gōn).
From Latin lexis, from Ancient Greek λέξις (léxis, “word”) + -al.
Borrowed from Latin lichen, from Ancient Greek λειχήν (leikhḗn).
Inherited from Middle French lyon, from Old French lion, a semi-learned borrowing from Latin leōnem, from Ancient Greek λέων (léōn).
From Latin lochāgus, from Ancient Greek λοχᾱγός (lokhāgós).
Learned borrowing from Latin logica, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek λογική (logikḗ), ellipsis of λογικὴ τέχνη (logikḕ tékhnē, “the art of reasoning”).
Learned borrowing from Latin logicus, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek λογικός (logikós).

parole.significato: lochus (a military unit headed by a lochagus)
parole.testo: From Latin lochus, from Ancient Greek λόχος (lókhos).
Borrowed from Latin lōtus, from Ancient Greek λωτός (lōtós).

From Latin lyceum, from Ancient Greek Λύκειον (Lúkeion) (the name of a gymnasium, or athletic training facility, near Athens where Aristotle established his school), from Λύκειος (Lúkeios, of uncertain meaning; possibly “wolf-killing”, “Lycian” or “luminous”), epithet of Apollo.
Inherited from Middle French lycee, from Latin Lycēus, from Ancient Greek Λύκειος (Lúkeios, of uncertain meaning; possibly “wolf-killing”, “Lycian” or “luminous”), epithet of Apollo.
From Latin Lycēus [from Ancient Greek Λύκειος (Lúkeios, of uncertain meaning; possibly “wolf-killing”, “Lycian” or “luminous”), epithet of Apollo] + -en.
From Latin lympha, from Ancient Greek νύμφη (númphē).
Borrowed from Latin, from Ancient Greek λύγξ (lúnx). Doublet of once.
Borrowed from Latin lepra, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek λέπρα (lépra).
Borrowed from Latin māchinārī (“scheme, plot”), a verb based on Latin māchina (“machine, contrivance, device, scheme”), an early borrowing from Ancient Greek. See also machine.
Learned borrowing from Latin magicus, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek μαγικός (magikós). By surface analysis, magie + -ique.
From Latin malaxāre, from Ancient Greek μαλάσσω (malássō).

parole.significato: Catapult, mangonel, machine for throwing rocks.
parole.testo: From Old French mangonel, from Latin manganellus, manganum, from Ancient Greek μάγγανον (mánganon).
Borrowed from Latin mania or Ancient Greek μανία (manía, “madness”).
Inherited from Old French marbre, from Latin marmor, from Ancient Greek μάρμαρος (mármaros).
From Latin margarīta (“pearl”), from Ancient Greek μαργαρίτης (margarítēs).
Borrowed from Latin martyrium, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek μαρτύριον (martúrion).
From Latin massa, from Ancient Greek μᾶζα (mâza, “bread”).
Old French mastic, from Latin mastiche, from Ancient Greek μαστίχη (mastíkhē), from μαστιχάω (mastikháō, “to chew”).
Learned borrowing from Latin mathēmaticus, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek μαθηματικός (mathēmatikós, “fond of learning”).
Semi-learned borrowing from Latin Messiās, from Ancient Greek Μεσσίας (Messías), from Aramaic [Term?].
From Latin mimus, from Ancient Greek μῖμος (mîmos).

Ultimately from Latin myrobalanum, from Ancient Greek μυροβάλανος (murobálanos). First attested in 1838. Likely originates as Mirobolan, the name of a medicine in Crispin medecin, a 1680 comedy by Hauteroche, a humorous reinterpretation/respelling of myrobolan (“myrobalan, a medicinal plant”) as pre
Borrowed from Latin molossus, short for molossus canis (literally “Molossus dog”), from Ancient Greek Μολοσσός (Molossós, “of Molossus (an area known for its guard-dogs)”).
Borrowed from Latin monastērium, from Ancient Greek μοναστήριον (monastḗrion, “hermit's cell”), from μόνος (mónos, “alone”). Doublet of moutier (Old French mostier).
Learned borrowing from Latin monochordon, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek μονόχορδον (monókhordon).
Learned borrowing from Latin monōdia, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek μονῳδία (monōidía).
Borrowed from Latin monophthongos or monophthongus, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek μονόφθογγος (monóphthongos, “monophthong”).
Borrowed from Latin monopōlium.
Inherited from Middle French moustier, from Old French mostier, inherited from Latin monastērium, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek μοναστήριον (monastḗrion). Doublet of monastère.

From Old French muguete, muguede (as in nois muguete (“nutmeg”)), from Latin muscāta, feminine of muscātus (“musky”), from Ancient Greek μόσχος (móskhos), from Middle Persian mwšk' (/⁠*mušk⁠/, “musk”), ultimately from Sanskrit मुष्क (muṣka, “testicle”), the shape of the gland being similar.
Inherited from Old French mulet, from Latin mullus, from Ancient Greek μύλλος (múllos).
Learned borrowing from Latin murēna, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek μύραινα (múraina).
Inherited from Old French musique, borrowed from Latin mūsica, borrowed from Ancient Greek μουσική (mousikḗ, “art of the Muses”), derived from Μοῦσα (Moûsa, “Muse”).
Learned borrowing from Latin mūsīvum.

parole.significato: museum (a building or institution dedicated to the acquisition, conservation, study, exhibition, and educational interp…
parole.testo: From Latin mūsēum (“library, study”), from Ancient Greek Μουσεῖον (Mouseîon), shrine of the Muses (Μοῦσα (Moûsa)).
From Middle French myrobolan, from Old French mirabolan, from Latin myrobalanum, myrobalanus, from Ancient Greek μυροβάλανος (murobálanos).

parole.significato: myrrh (dried sap of the myrrha tree)
parole.testo: From Latin myrrha, from Ancient Greek μύρρα (múrrha), from a Semitic root M-R-R meaning bitter, akin to Arabic مُرّ (murr, “bitter”), Hebrew מֹר (mor, “bitterness, acrimony”).
Borrowed from Latin myrtus.
Borrowed from Latin mysticus.
Inherited from Middle French mystere, a borrowing from Latin mystērium, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek μῠστήρῐον (mŭstḗrĭon). See also métier.
From Latin mythos m, from Ancient Greek μῦθος m (mûthos).
Borrowed from Latin metrum, itself from Ancient Greek μέτρον (métron).

parole.significato: mechanical (of or pertaining to a machine)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin mechanicus (“of or belonging to machines”), itself borrowed from Ancient Greek μηχανικός (mēkhanikós, “pertaining to machines”), from μηχανή (mēkhanḗ, “a machine, contrivance”) (whence machine).
From Méduse (“Medusa (Greek mythology)”), from Latin Medusa, from Ancient Greek Μέδουσα (Médousa), from μέδω (médō, “rule over”).
Borrowed from Latin megaricus, from Ancient Greek Μεγαρικός (Megarikós).
After Mégère (“Megaera”), deity of vengeance, borrowed from Latin Megaera, from Ancient Greek Μέγαιρα (Mégaira). Compare Portuguese and Italian megera.

parole.significato: Melanchlaeni (a Scythian tribe which dwelt in Pontus)
parole.testo: From Latin Melanchlaenī, from Ancient Greek Μελάγχλαινοι (Melánkhlainoi).

parole.significato: melody (sequence of notes that makes up a musical phrase)
parole.testo: From Latin melodia, from Ancient Greek μελῳδίᾱ (melōidíā).
From Latin maenas (“bacchant”), from Ancient Greek μαινάς (mainás, “raving, frantic”), from Ancient Greek μαίνεσθαι (maínesthai, “be furious”).
Borrowed from Latin metallum (“metal, mine, quarry, mineral”), from Ancient Greek μέταλλον (métallon, “mine, quarry, metal”), of unknown origin.
From Latin metamorphosis (“change of shape”), from Ancient Greek μεταμόρφωσις (metamórphōsis), from μετά (metá, “change”) + μορφή (morphḗ, “form”).
Learned borrowing from Latin metaphora, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek μεταφορά (metaphorá).

Inherited from Middle French method, borrowed from Latin methodus, from Ancient Greek μέθοδος (méthodos, “pursuit of knowledge, investigation, mode of prosecuting such inquiry, system”), from μετά (metá, “after”) + ὁδός (hodós, “way, motion, journey”).
Borrowed from Latin metopa, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek μετόπη (metópē).

parole.significato: metic (resident alien who did not have the rights of a citizen and who paid a tax for the right to live there)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin metoecus, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek μέτοικος (métoikos).

parole.significato: narcissus (any of several bulbous flowering plants, of the genus Narcissus)
parole.testo: From Latin narcissus, from Ancient Greek νάρκισσος (nárkissos).

parole.significato: nauclerus (a shipmaster, a shipowner, a skipper)
parole.testo: From Latin nauclērus, from Ancient Greek ναύκληρος (naúklēros).
Learned borrowing from Latin naumachia, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ναυμαχία (naumakhía).
Borrowed from Latin nausea, nausia, from Ancient Greek ναυσία (nausía, “seasickness”), from ναῦς (naûs, “ship”).
Learned borrowing from Latin nauticus, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ναυτικός (nautikós).
From Latin nectar, from Ancient Greek νέκταρ (néktar), from Proto-Indo-European *néḱtr̥h₂, derived from the roots *neḱ- (“to perish, disappear”) and *terh₂- (“to overcome”).
From Latin nitrum (“niter, natron”), from Ancient Greek νίτρον (nítron). Ultimately from Egyptian nṯrj (“natron”).
Inherited from Middle French, derived from Latin numismat- + -ique; ultimately from Ancient Greek νόμισμα (nómisma).
Inherited from Middle French, from Old French nimphe, borrowed from Latin nympha or nymphē (“nymph”), from Ancient Greek νύμφη (númphē, “young woman, nymph”).
Borrowed from Latin nymphaea, from Ancient Greek νυμφαία (numphaía).
From Latin Nereis, from Ancient Greek Νηρηΐς (Nērēḯs). By surface analysis, Nérée + -ide.
Learned borrowing from Latin obolus, from Ancient Greek ὀβολός (obolós).

parole.significato: obelisk (a tall, square, tapered, stone monolith topped with a pyramidal point)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin obeliscus (“obelisk”), itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ὀβελίσκος (obelískos).
From Latin octō (“eight”) or Ancient Greek ὀκτώ (oktṓ, “eight”).

parole.significato: an ocean (one of the large bodies of water separating the continents)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin ōceanus.
From Latin Oceanis, from Ancient Greek Ὠκεανίς (Ōkeanís). By surface analysis, Océan + -ide.
From Middle French ode, from Latin ōda, from Ancient Greek ᾠδή (ōidḗ).
Inherited from Old French olifan.
Learned borrowing from Latin onager, borrowed from Ancient Greek ὄναγρος (ónagros, “wild ass”), from ὄνος (ónos, “ass, donkey”) + ᾰ̓́γρῐος (ắgrĭos, “wild”).
From Latin opium, from Ancient Greek ὄπιον (ópion).
Borrowed from Latin opopanax, from Hellenistic Greek ὀποπάναξ (opopánax), from Ancient Greek ὀπός (opós, “vegetable juice”) + πάναξ (pánax).
From Latin orchis (wrongly interpreting orchid- as the stem), from Ancient Greek ὄρχις (órkhis, “orchid, testicle”) + -ectomie.
Borrowed from Latin organum, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ὄργανον (órganon, “organ, instrument, tool”). Doublet of orgue, an older borrowing.
Borrowed from Latin orgia, a neuter plural reinterpreted as a feminine singular; itself from Ancient Greek ὄργια (órgia).
Borrowed from Latin organum, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ὄργανον (órganon). Doublet of organe, a later borrowing.
Learned borrowing from Latin orichalcum, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ὀρείχαλκος (oreíkhalkos).
From Old French orfelin, by dissimilation from orfenin, diminutive of orfene, from ecclesiastical Latin orphanus, from Ancient Greek ὀρφανός (orphanós).
Borrowed from Latin orthographia, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ὀρθογρᾰφῐ́ᾱ (orthogrăphĭ́ā).

parole.significato: oxymoron (figure of speech in which two words or phrases with opposing meanings are used together intentionally for eff…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin oxymōrus, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ὀξύμωρος (oxúmōros).
From Middle French, from Latin Palaestinus, from Ancient Greek Παλαιστινός (Palaistinós).
From Latin palimpsēstus, from Ancient Greek παλίμψηστος (palímpsēstos, “scraped again”).
Borrowed from Latin panacēa, from Ancient Greek πανάκεια (panákeia).
From Latin pancratium (“pankration”), from Ancient Greek παγκράτιον (pankrátion, “all powers; pankration”).
Borrowed from Latin pancreas, from Ancient Greek πάγκρεας (pánkreas).
Borrowed from Latin pandura, from Ancient Greek πᾰνδοῦρᾰ (păndoûră).
Borrowed from Latin papȳrus, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek πάπυρος (pápuros).
Inherited from Middle French paradis, from Old French paradis, borrowed from Latin paradīsus, from Ancient Greek παράδεισος (parádeisos), ultimately from Proto-Iranian *paridayjah. Doublet of parvis.
Borrowed from Latin paragraphus, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek παράγραφος (parágraphos). Doublet of paraphe.
Borrowed from Latin parallēlogrammum, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek παραλληλόγραμμον (parallēlógrammon).
Borrowed from Latin parallēlepipedum, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek παραλληλεπίπεδον (parallēlepípedon).
Borrowed from Latin paralysis, from Ancient Greek παράλυσις (parálusis, “palsy”).
Borrowed from Latin paralyticus, from Ancient Greek παραλυτικός (paralutikós, “paralyzed”).
From parasite, from Latin parasitus 'parasite', ultimately from Ancient Greek.
Borrowed from Latin parasītus, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek παράσιτος (parásitos).
Learned borrowing from Latin paronomasia, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek παρονομασία (paronomasía).
Inherited from Middle French Parthe, from Latin Parthus, from Ancient Greek Πάρθος (Párthos).
Borrowed from Latin pathēticus, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek παθητικός (pathētikós).

Inherited from Old French peine, from Latin poena, from Ancient Greek ποινή (poinḗ, “penalty, fine, bloodmoney”). Cognate with Spanish pena, Italian pena, Portuguese pena. False friend of Spanish peine (“comb”).
From Latin pentēcontarchia, from Ancient Greek πεντηκονταρχία (pentēkontarkhía). By surface analysis, pentécontarque + -ie.

parole.significato: pentecontarch (the commander of a platoon of fifty men)
parole.testo: From Latin pentēcontarchus, from Ancient Greek πεντηκόνταρχος (pentēkóntarkhos, literally “commander of fifty”).
Inherited from Old French perche, from Latin perca, from Ancient Greek πέρκη (pérkē).
Inherited from Old French perdriz, from Latin perdīcem, from Ancient Greek πέρδιξ (pérdix).

parole.significato: Pergamene (native or inhabitant of Pergamum) (usually male)
parole.testo: From Latin Pergamēnus, from Ancient Greek Περγαμηνός (Pergamēnós).
Inherited from Middle French Perse, from Latin Persēs/Persa, from Ancient Greek Πέρσης (Pérsēs), from Old Persian 𐎱𐎠𐎼𐎿 (p-a-r-s /⁠pārsa⁠/).

Inherited from Old French persil, peresil, perresil, inherited from Latin petroselīnum (possibly through a Vulgar Latin *petrosīnu, compare Sicilian pitrusinu and the Old French variant persin, later with the suffix -il; or through Early Medieval Latin petrosilio), itself from Ancient Greek πετροσέλ
Inherited from Middle French phalle, from Latin phallus, from Ancient Greek φαλλός (phallós).
From Latin phallicus, from Ancient Greek φαλλικός (phallikós), from φαλλός (phallós) + -ικός (-ikós). By surface analysis, phalle + -ique or phall(us) + -ique.
From Latin phallobata, adapted form of phallobatēs, from Ancient Greek φαλλοβάτης (phallobátēs). By surface analysis, phallo- + -bate.
From Latin phallophorus, from Ancient Greek φαλλοφόρος (phallophóros). By surface analysis, phallo- + -phore.
From Latin phallophoria n pl, from Ancient Greek φαλλοφόρια n pl (phallophória). By surface analysis, phallo- + -phories.
Borrowed from Latin pharus, itself from Ancient Greek Φάρος (Pháros).
From Latin pharetra, from Ancient Greek φαρέτρα (pharétra).
Borrowed from Latin Phaëtōn, from the Ancient Greek Φᾰέθων (Phăéthōn).
Inherited from Middle French philosophe, from Latin philosophus, from Ancient Greek φιλόσοφος (philósophos).
Inherited from Old French philosophie, from Latin philosophia, from Ancient Greek φῐλοσοφῐ́ᾱ (phĭlosophĭ́ā); compare philosophe.

parole.significato: philter (a kind of potion, charm, or drug intended to make the drinker fall in love with the giver)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin philtrum, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek φίλτρον (phíltron). Unrelated to filtre.
Inherited from Middle French phoque f, focque m, borrowed from Latin phōca, from Ancient Greek φώκη (phṓkē). Cognate with Italian foca f and Spanish foca f.
From Latin phōsphorus, from Ancient Greek φωσφόρος (phōsphóros, “the bearer of light”), from φῶς (phôs, “light”) + φέρω (phérō, “to bear, to carry”).
From Latin phrasis (“diction”), from Ancient Greek φράσις (phrásis, “manner of expression”), from φράζω (phrázō, “to tell, express”).
Learned borrowing from Latin phthisis, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek φθίσις (phthísis).
From Latin phyllon, from Ancient Greek φύλλον (phúllon, “leaf”).
Inherited from Middle French pierre, from Old French pierre, from Latin petra.
Borrowed from Latin pinacotheca, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek πινακοθήκη (pinakothḗkē).
Inherited from Old French pyoine (with epenthetic /-v-/), borrowed from Latin paeōnia, borrowed from Ancient Greek παιωνία (paiōnía, “peony”).
Inherited from Old French place, from Latin platea, from Ancient Greek πλατεῖα (plateîa).
From Old French plane, from Latin platanus, from Ancient Greek πλάτανος (plátanos), from πλατύς (platús, “wide, broad”).
From Latin planēta, from Ancient Greek πλανήτης (planḗtēs, “wanderer, planet”), from πλανάω (planáō, “to wander”).
From Middle French plastique, borrowed from Latin plasticus. Doublet of plastic.
Borrowed from Latin platanus, from Ancient Greek πλάτανος (plátanos). Doublet of the inherited plane, now a regional term.
Learned borrowing from Latin pleonasmus, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek πλεονασμός (pleonasmós).
Learned borrowing from Latin pneumaticus, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek πνευματικός (pneumatikós, “relating to wind or air”), from πνεῦμα (pneûma, “wind, air, breath, spirit”).
Inherited from Old French pois, from earlier peis from Latin pisum, from Ancient Greek πίσος / πίσον (písos / píson).
Inherited from Old French peivre, peivere, from Latin piper.
Learned borrowing from Latin polīticus, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek πολιτικός (politikós).
From Latin polygamia, from Ancient Greek πολυγαμία (polugamía).
Learned borrowing from Latin polygōnum, from Ancient Greek πολύγωνον (polúgōnon).

From Middle French pompe, from Old French pompe (“extravagant ceremony, pomp”), from Latin pompa (“display, procession, parade”), from Ancient Greek πομπή (pompḗ, “procession, send-off”), from πέμπω (pémpō, “to send”).
From Old French pore, from Latin porus, from Ancient Greek πόρος (póros, “passage”).
Ultimately borrowed from Latin polypūs, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek πολύπους (polúpous). Doublet of polype and pieuvre.
Inherited from Old French, from Latin purpura, from Ancient Greek πορφύρα (porphúra).
From Latin poēma, from Ancient Greek ποίημα (poíēma).
Borrowed from Latin poēta, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ποιητής (poiētḗs).
Learned borrowing from Latin poēticus, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ποιητικός (poiētikós).
From Latin presbyterālis, from Ancient Greek πρέσβυς (présbus, “old”).
Borrowed from Latin priapismus, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek πριαπισμός (priapismós).
Inherited from Middle French probleme, a borrowing from Latin problēma, from Ancient Greek πρόβλημα (próblēma, “obstacle”).
Inherited from Old French prologue, a borrowing from Latin prologus, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek πρόλογος (prólogos).

parole.significato: prophet (one who speaks by divine inspiration)
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle French prophete, from Old French prophete, from Latin prophēta, from Ancient Greek προφήτης (prophḗtēs, “one who speaks for a god”), from πρό (pró, “before”) + φημί (phēmí, “to tell”).
From Latin prophētīa, from Ancient Greek προφητεία (prophēteía, “prophecy”).
Inherited from Old French prophetisier, from Latin prophētizāre, from Ancient Greek προφητίζω (prophētízō, “to prophesy”). By surface analysis, prophète + -iser.
Borrowed from Latin propolis, from Hellenistic Ancient Greek πρόπολις (própolis, “suburb; propolis”), from Ancient Greek προ- (pro-, “pro-”) + πόλις (pólis, “city”).
Borrowed from Latin prosōdia, from Ancient Greek προσῳδία (prosōidía, “song sung to music; pronunciation of syllable”), from πρός (prós, “to”) + ᾠδή (ōidḗ, “song”).
Learned borrowing from Latin prosopopoeia, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek προσωποποιΐα (prosōpopoiḯa).
Borrowed from Latin prōtotypus, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek πρωτότυπος (prōtótupos).
Borrowed from Latin proxenēta, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek προξενητής (proxenētḗs).
From Latin prytanis, from Ancient Greek πρύτανις (prútanis).

parole.significato: prytaneum (the town hall in an Ancient Greek city)
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle French prytanee, from Latin prytanēum, from Ancient Greek πρυτανεῖον (prutaneîon). By surface analysis, prytane + -ée.

Inherited from Middle French prestre, from Old French prestre (nominative form, compare provoire), from Latin presbyter, from Ancient Greek πρεσβύτερος (presbúteros), from πρέσβυς (présbus, “elder, older”). Doublet of praire and presbytre, a recent borrowing.

From Middle French psaulme, from Old French psalme, salme, borrowed from Latin psalmus, from Ancient Greek ψαλμός (psalmós). The p- was silent well into Modern French, but later came to be pronounced by analogy with learned words with ps- which had since been borrowed from Greek.
Learned borrowing from Latin psȳchopompus, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ψῡχοπομπός (psūkhopompós).

parole.significato: during Roman times, a member of a tribe from Libya who were said to charm snakes and be immune to their venom
parole.testo: From Latin Psylli (“Psylles”), from Ancient Greek Ψύλλοι (Psúlloi).
Borrowed from Latin Ptolemaeus, itself from Ancient Greek Πτολεμαῖος (Ptolemaîos).
Learned borrowing from Latin pȳgargus, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek πῡ́γᾰργος (pū́gărgos).
Learned borrowing from Latin pȳramis, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek πυραμίς (puramís).
From Latin pyrēum, from Ancient Greek πυρεῖον (pureîon).

parole.significato: only used in monts Pyrénées m pl (“Pyrenean mounts”) and montagnes Pyrénées f (“Pyrenean mountains”)
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle French pyrenee, from Latin Pyrenaeus (“Pyrenean”), from Ancient Greek Πῡρηναῖος (Pūrēnaîos), from Πῡρήνη (Pūrḗnē, “Pyrene”) + -αῖος (-aîos). By surface analysis, Pyrène + -ée.
Inherited from Middle French pæan, from Latin paean, from Ancient Greek παιάν (paián).
Learned borrowing from Latin paedagogicus, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek παιδαγωγικός (paidagōgikós), from παιδαγωγός (paidagōgós, “teacher, tutor”). By surface analysis, pédagogie + -ique.
Inherited from Middle French pedagoge, pedagogue, borrowed from Latin paedagōgus, from Ancient Greek παιδᾰγωγός (paidăgōgós).
From Latin pelagicus, from Ancient Greek πελαγικός (pelagikós).
Borrowed from Latin peplum, from Ancient Greek πέπλων (péplōn), neuter of πέπλος (péplos).
From Latin pericarpium, from Ancient Greek περικάρπιον (perikárpion, “pod, husk, shell”), from περί (perí, “around”) + καρπός (karpós, “fruit”).

parole.significato: of Aristotle and his philosophy; Peripatetic
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin peripatēticus, from Ancient Greek περιπατητικός (peripatētikós, “given to walking around”), from περιπατέω (peripatéō, “to walk around”), from περί (perí, “around”) + πατέω (patéō, “to walk”).
Borrowed from Latin periphrasis < Ancient Greek περίφρασις (períphrasis).
Learned borrowing from Latin peripherīa, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek περιφέρεια (periphéreia).
Inherited from Middle French pole, from Old French pole, from Latin polus, from Ancient Greek πόλος (pólos).
From Latin rhaponticum, literally rha (“rhubarb”) ponticum (“Pontic; of the Black Sea”), from Ancient Greek ῥῆον (rhêon, “rhubarb”) and Ancient Greek Πόντος (Póntos, “Black Sea”).
From a feminine form of Old French rafne, ravene, from Latin raphanus, from Ancient Greek ῥάφανος (rháphanos, “radish, cabbage”).
Borrowed from Latin rhīnocerōs, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ῥινόκερως (rhinókerōs).
Borrowed from Latin rhododendron, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ῥοδόδενδρον (rhodódendron).
Learned borrowing from Latin rhētoricus, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ῥητορικός (rhētorikós).
From Old French rhetorique, a borrowing from Latin rhētorica, from Ancient Greek ῥητορική (rhētorikḗ), ellipsis of ῥητορικὴ τέχνη (rhētorikḕ tékhnē).
From post-Classical Latin Rōmaeus [calque of Ancient Greek Ῥωμαῖος (Rhōmaîos)] + -en. By surface analysis, Rome + -éen.
From post-Classical Latin Rōmaeus [calque of Ancient Greek Ῥωμαῖος (Rhōmaîos)] + -en. By surface analysis, Rome + -éen.
Inherited from Old French rue, rude, from Latin rūta, from Ancient Greek ῥυτή (rhutḗ).
Learned borrowing from Latin rhythmus, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ῥυθμός (rhuthmós).

Borrowed from Latin sabbatum, from Ancient Greek σάββατον (sábbaton, “Sabbath”), from Hebrew שבת (shabát, “Sabbath”). In regards to the semantic evolution to "witches' meeting" compare with ramdam, brouhaha. See also samedi.
From Latin sabbatismus (“Sabbath observance", "Sabbath-keeping, Sabbathkeeping”), from Ancient Greek σαββατισμός (sabbatismós).
Inherited from Old French sac, from Latin saccus, from Ancient Greek σάκκος (sákkos, “sack, bag; sackcloth”), ultimately from Semitic.
Borrowed from Latin sambūca, from Ancient Greek σαμβύκη (sambúkē), ultimately from Aramaic סַבְּכָא (sabbəḵā).
Inherited from Middle French scarabée, borrowed from Latin scarabaeus, from Ancient Greek κάραβος (kárabos). Compare the inherited doublet escarbot.
From Latin scarus (also genus name Scarus), from Ancient Greek σκάρος (skáros).
Borrowed from Latin scēptrum, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek σκῆπτρον (skêptron).
Borrowed from Latin schēma, from Ancient Greek σχῆμα (skhêma, “form, shape”).
Learned borrowing from Latin scincos, from Ancient Greek σκίγκος (skínkos).
Inherited from Middle French scholastique, borrowed from Latin scholasticus, from Ancient Greek σχολαστικός (skholastikós).

parole.significato: scoliosis (condition where there is abnormal lateral curvature of the spine)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin scoliōsis, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek σκολίωσις (skolíōsis, “twisting; torsion”).
Inherited from Middle French scolopendre, from Latin scolopendra/scolopendrium, from Ancient Greek σκολόπενδρα (skolópendra)/σκολόπένδριο (skolópéndrio).
Borrowed from Latin scorpiōnem.

parole.significato: scyphus (a kind of large drinking cup used in Ancient Greece and Ancient Rome, especially by poor people)
parole.testo: From Latin scyphus, from Ancient Greek σκῠ́φος (skŭ́phos).
From Latin Scytha, from Ancient Greek Σκύθης (Skúthēs).
Inherited from Middle French scene (1486), borrowed from Latin sc(a)ena, from Ancient Greek σκηνή (skēnḗ).

parole.significato: stage, scenic (of or relating to a theatrical scene)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin scēnicus, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek σκηνικός (skēnikós). By surface analysis, scène + -ique.
From Latin scaenographia, from Ancient Greek σκηνογραφία (skēnographía).
From Latin sēpia, from Ancient Greek σηπία (sēpía).
Inherited from Latin sagēna, from Ancient Greek σαγήνη (sagḗnē).
From Latin silūrus, in turn from Ancient Greek.
From Middle French silene, from Latin sīlēnus (“silen”), named after Sīlēnus (“Silenus”), from Ancient Greek Σῑληνός (Sīlēnós).
From Latin Sīlēnicus, from Ancient Greek Σῑληνῐκός (Sīlēnĭkós). By surface analysis, Silène + -ique.
From Latin Sina (“China”) + Ancient Greek ἄνθρωπος (ánthrōpos, “human”).
From Middle French siphon, from Old French sifon, from Latin sīphō from Ancient Greek σίφων (síphōn, “pipe, tube”), of unknown ultimate origin.
Borrowed from Latin sirēna, from Latin Sīrēn, from Ancient Greek Σειρήν (Seirḗn). Cf. also Old French sereine. Doublet of serin.
Borrowed from Latin sīstrum, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek σεῖστρον (seîstron).
From Latin Smyrna, from Ancient Greek Σμύρνα (Smúrna).
From Smyrne + -éen, modelled after Latin Smyrnaeus, from Ancient Greek Σμυρναῖος (Smurnaîos).
From Smyrne + -éen, modelled after Latin Smyrnaeus, from Ancient Greek Σμυρναῖος (Smurnaîos).
Inherited from Old French Sodomite, from Latin sodomīta, from Ancient Greek σοδομίτης (sodomítēs).
Borrowed from Latin soloecismus.
Learned borrowing from Latin sophisma (“fallacy, sophism”), itself borrowed from Ancient Greek σόφῐσμᾰ (sóphĭsmă).
Borrowed from Latin sophistes, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek σοφιστής (sophistḗs).
Learned borrowing from Latin sophisticus, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek σοφιστικός (sophistikós); morphologically, from sophiste + -ique.
From Latin spasmus, from Ancient Greek σπασμός (spasmós, “spasm, convulsion”).
Borrowed from Latin spatha, from Ancient Greek σπάθη (spáthē). Doublet of épée, which was inherited.
Borrowed from Latin sperma, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek σπέρμα (spérma).

parole.significato: sphinx (a sculpture representing the Sphinx of Greek mythology)
parole.testo: From Latin sphingem f, from Ancient Greek Σφίγξ f (Sphínx). Cognate with Italian sfinge f, Portuguese esfinge f, Spanish esfinge f.
Unadapted borrowing from Latin sphinx f, from Ancient Greek Σφίγξ (Sphínx).
Learned borrowing from Latin sphaericus. By surface analysis, sphère + -ique.
From Latin spira, from Ancient Greek σπεῖρα (speîra).
Learned borrowing from Latin spora, from Ancient Greek σπορά (sporá).
From Middle French scelette, a learned borrowing from Latin sceletus, from Ancient Greek σκελετός (skeletós, “dried up, withered, dried body, parched, mummy”).
From Latin stadium, from Ancient Greek στάδιον (stádion), neuter form of στάδιος (stádios, “stable, firm”), from Proto-Indo-European *steh₂- (“to be standing”).
Borrowed from Latin Stentōr, from Ancient Greek Στέντωρ (Sténtōr), the name of a herald in the Iliad who had a loud voice.
Learned borrowing from Latin stigma, stigmatis, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek στίγμα, στίγματος (stígma, stígmatos).
Borrowed from Latin stōicus, from Ancient Greek Στωϊκός (Stōïkós).
Inherited from Middle French stratageme, from Old French stratageme, a borrowing from Latin strategema, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek στρατήγημα (stratḗgēma).

parole.significato: general (leader or commander of an army)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin stratēgus, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek στρατηγός (stratēgós, “general”).

Inherited from Old French strategie, from Latin strategia, a borrowing from Ancient Greek στρατηγία (stratēgía, “office of general, command, generalship”), from στρατηγός (stratēgós, “the leader or commander of an army, a general”), from στρατός (stratós, “army”) + ἄγω (ágō, “to lead, to conduct”).
Borrowed from Latin stropha, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek στροφή (strophḗ).
Borrowed from Latin strīga, from strīx, from Ancient Greek στρίξ (stríx). Compare Old French estrie, which was the inherited form.
From Latin stylobata, from Ancient Greek στυλοβάτης (stulobátēs). By surface analysis, style + -bate.
Learned borrowing from Latin stypticus, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek στυπτικός (stuptikós), from στύφω (stúphō, “to contract”).
Borrowed from Latin syllaba.
Borrowed from Latin symbolum, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek σύμβολον (súmbolon).
Borrowed from Latin symphōnia, from Ancient Greek συμφωνία (sumphōnía). Doublet of chifonie.

parole.significato: any one of the Symplegades (a pair of rocks at the Bosphorus that clashed together whenever a vessel passed through)
parole.testo: From Latin Symplēgas, from Ancient Greek Συμπληγάς (Sumplēgás).
From Middle French (sinthome, Bernard de Gordon). Borrowed from Latin symptōma, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek σύμπτωμα (súmptōma).
From Middle French symmetrie, from Latin symmetria, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek συμμετρία (summetría).

parole.significato: synagogue (a place of worship for Jews)
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle French synagogue, Old French synagoge, borrowed from Latin synagōga, from Ancient Greek σῠνᾰγωγή (sŭnăgōgḗ, “assembly, gathering”), from συνάγω (sunágō, “to gather together”), from σῠ́ν (sŭ́n, “with, together”) & ᾰ̓́γω (ắgō, “to lead”).
Borrowed from Latin synchronus, from Ancient Greek σύγχρονος (súnkhronos).

parole.significato: synchysis (confused arrangement of words in a sentence)
parole.testo: From Latin synchysis, from Ancient Greek σύγχυσις (súnkhusis).
Learned borrowing from Latin syncretismus, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek συγκρητισμός (sunkrētismós).

parole.significato: synecdoche (figure of speech that uses the name of a part of something to represent the whole, or the whole to represen…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin synecdochē, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek συνεκδοχή (sunekdokhḗ, “receiving together”).
From Latin synodus, from Ancient Greek σύνοδος (súnodos, “assembly, meeting”), from σύν (sún, “with”) (English syn-) + ὁδός (hodós, “way, path”).

parole.significato: synaeresis (contraction of two vowels into a diphthong or a long vowel)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin synaeresis, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek συναίρεσις (sunaíresis).
Learned borrowing from Latin Syriacus, from Ancient Greek Συριακός (Suriakós), from Συρία (Suría).
From Latin Syriarcha, from Ancient Greek Συριάρχης (Suriárkhēs).
Inherited from Middle French syringe, from Latin sȳringem, accusative of sȳrinx, from Ancient Greek σῦριγξ (sûrinx). Cognate with Italian siringe, Portuguese siringe, Spanish siringe.

parole.significato: arrangement of colonnade where the space between columns is twice the diameter of each
parole.testo: From Latin systylos, from Ancient Greek σύστυλος (sústulos) composed of σύν (sún) and στῦλος (stûlos).
Borrowed from Latin syzygia, from Ancient Greek συζυγία (suzugía).
Inherited from Old French teie, inherited from Latin thēca, itself from Ancient Greek θήκη (thḗkē). Doublet of thèque and -thèque.

parole.significato: a talent (an obsolete unit of weight or money)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin talentum (“a Grecian weight; a talent of money”), itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek τάλαντον (tálanton, “balance; a particular weight, especially of gold; sum of money; a talent”).

parole.significato: female native or inhabitant of Taprobana
parole.testo: From Latin Tāprobana, from Ancient Greek Ταπροβάνη (Taprobánē).
Borrowed from Latin thalamegus, itself from Ancient Greek θᾰλᾰμηγός (thălămēgós).
From Latin thunnus, thynnus (itself from Ancient Greek θύννος (thúnnos)), possibly through the intermediate of Old Occitan ton.
From Latin thōrax, from Ancient Greek θώραξ (thṓrax, “a breastplate, cuirass, corslet”).
From Latin threnus, itself from Ancient Greek θρῆνος (thrênos), θρέομαι (thréomai).
Borrowed from Latin thymum.
Inherited from Middle French thyrse, borrowed from Latin thyrsus, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek θύρσος (thúrsos). Doublet of torse, a borrowing from Italian.
Inherited from Middle French theme, from Old French teme, tesme, a learned borrowing from Latin thema, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek θέμα (théma).
Learned borrowing from Latin thesis, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek θέσις (thésis).
From Latin Thēbaicus, from Ancient Greek Θηϐαϊκός (Thēbaïkós).
Inherited from Middle French theologie, from Old French theologie, from Latin theologia, from Ancient Greek θεολογία (theología). By surface analysis, théo- + -logie.

Borrowed from Latin theoria, from Ancient Greek θεωρία (theōría, “contemplation, speculation, a looking at, things looked at”), from θεωρέω (theōréō, “to look at, view, consider, examine”), from θεωρός (theōrós, “spectator”), from θέα (théa, “view”) + ὁράω (horáō, “to see, to look”).
Borrowed from Latin theōricus, from Ancient Greek θεωρικός (theōrikós). By surface analysis, théorie + -ique.
Inherited from Middle French théorème, a borrowing from Latin theōrēma, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek θεώρημᾰ (theṓrēmă).
Borrowed from Latin theōrēticus, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek θεωρητικός (theōrētikós). By surface analysis, théorie + -(et)ique.
Unadapted borrowing from Latin thēsaurus (“treasure; hoard”), from Ancient Greek θησαυρός (thēsaurós, “storehouse; treasure”). See also the doublet trésor.

parole.significato: theatre (venue for performing plays and drama; performing art form)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin theātrum, from Ancient Greek θέατρον (théatron, “a place for viewing”), from θεάομαι (theáomai, “to see, to watch, to observe”).
Inherited from Middle French tigre, from Old French tigre, from Latin tigris.
From Latin tisana, ptisana, from Ancient Greek πτισάνη (ptisánē, “peeled barley, barley gruel”), related to πτίσσειν (ptíssein, “to peel”).
From Latin Titanis, from Ancient Greek Τιτανίς (Titanís). By surface analysis, Titan + -ide.

parole.significato: Tokhar, Tocharian (any member of the Tochari, a people who inhabited Bactria)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Tocharus, from Ancient Greek Τόχαρος (Tókharos).
From Latin topographia, from Ancient Greek τοπογραφία (topographía), from τόπος (tópos, “place”) + γράφω (gráphō, “to write”). By surface analysis, topo- + -graphie.
Inherited from Old French tor, from Latin turrem, from Ancient Greek τύρρις (túrrhis), τύρσις (túrsis).

From Old French tragedie, a borrowing from Latin tragoedia, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek τραγῳδία (tragōidía, “epic play, tragedy”), from τράγος (trágos, “male goat”) + ᾠδή (ōidḗ, “song”), a reference to the goat-satyrs of the theatrical plays of the Dorians.
Learned borrowing from Latin trapezium.
Learned borrowing from Latin traumaticus, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek τραυματικός (traumatikós), from τραῦμα (traûma).
From Latin tri- (“three”) and Ancient Greek τρι- (tri-, “three”).

parole.significato: tribrach (metrical foot comprising three short syllables)
parole.testo: From Latin tribrachys, from Ancient Greek τρῐ́βρᾰχῠς (trĭ́brăkhŭs).
Borrowed from Latin tripodem, from Ancient Greek τρίπους (trípous). By surface analysis, tri- + -pode.
Learned borrowing from Latin Trītōn, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek Τρίτων (Trítōn).
Learned borrowing from Latin Trōglodytae (“cave-dwelling people”), from Ancient Greek τρωγλοδύτης (trōglodútēs, “one who dwells in holes”).

Inherited from Middle French trophée, borrowed from Latin trophaeum, tropaeum, from Ancient Greek τρόπαιον (trópaion, “monument of an enemy's defeat”), from neuter of τροπαῖος (tropaîos, “of defeat”), from τροπή (tropḗ, “a rout, a turning of an enemy”).

Inherited from Middle French tresor, from Old French tresor, from Vulgar Latin *tresaurus, a Gallo-Roman variant of Latin thēsaurus, from Ancient Greek θησαυρός (thēsaurós, “storehouse, treasure”). Eclipsed Old French escat (“treasure”), from Frankish *skatt. See also the doublet thésaurus.
Inherited from Middle French throne, from Old French trone, from Latin thronus, from Ancient Greek θρόνος (thrónos, “a seat, chair”).
From Latin typicus (“typical”), from Ancient Greek τύπος (túpos, “mark, impression, type”).
Inherited from Middle French tyran, borrowed from Latin tyrannus, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek τύραννος (túrannos). Replaced Old French tirant.
Learned borrowing from Latin tyrannicus, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek τυραννικός (turannikós). By surface analysis, tyran + -ique.
Borrowed from Latin Tyrrhēnus, from Ancient Greek Τυρρηνός (Turrhēnós).
From Latin tetrarchia, from Ancient Greek τετραρχία (tetrarkhía).
Learned borrowing from Latin tetrarchēs, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek τετράρχης (tetrárkhēs).
Borrowed from Latin zōna.
Learned borrowing from Latin zōophorus, from Ancient Greek ζωοφόρος (zōophóros).

parole.significato: zed, zee, The name of the Latin script letter Z/z.
parole.testo: Inherited from Old French zede, from Latin zēta (“Z, zeta”), borrowed from Ancient Greek ζῆτα (zêta, “zeta”). Doublet of zêta.
From Middle French zetha, borrowed from Latin zēta, from Ancient Greek ζῆτα (zêta). Doublet of zède.
Borrowed from Latin ebenus, from Ancient Greek ἔβενος (ébenos).
From Latin eclīpsis (“eclipse”), from Ancient Greek ἔκλειψις (ékleipsis, “eclipse”), from ἐκλείπω (ekleípō, “to abandon”), from ἐκ (ek, “out”) and λείπω (leípō, “to leave behind”).
From Latin eclīpticus, from Ancient Greek ἐκλειπτικός (ekleiptikós).
Inherited from Middle French eschole, from Old French escole, an early borrowing or semi-learned word taken from Latin schola, from Ancient Greek σχολή (skholḗ).
Learned borrowing from Latin oeconomus, from Ancient Greek οἰκονόμος (oikonómos), from οἶκος (oîkos, “house”) + νόμος (nómos, “law, rule”)
Borrowed from Latin oeconomia, from Ancient Greek οἰκονομία (oikonomía, “management of a household, administration”).
Learned borrowing from Latin aegis, aegidis, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek αἰγίς (aigís).
From Latin ecloga, from Ancient Greek ἐκλογή (eklogḗ, “selection”).
Borrowed from Latin aegaeus, from Ancient Greek Αἰγαῖος (Aigaîos).
From Latin Eleutherius, from Ancient Greek Ἐλευθέριος (Eleuthérios, literally “liberating”).
From Latin eleutheria, from Ancient Greek ἐλευθερία (eleuthería).

parole.significato: Eleutheria (an ancient Greek festival at Plataea in honor of Zeus Eleutherius)
parole.testo: From Latin Eleutheria, from Ancient Greek Ἐλευθέρια (Eleuthéria).
From Latin Elymus.
From Latin Elymus.

parole.significato: elegy (mournful or plaintive poem or song)
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle French elegie, a borrowing from Latin elegīa, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ἐλεγεία (elegeía).

parole.significato: elephant (large mammal of the family Elephantidae in the order Proboscidea)
